blocks.title: ABSTRACT
blocks.content:
The economic crisis has led to increased demand and reduced resources for health sectors. The trend for increasing 
healthcare costs to individuals, the health sector and wider society is significant. Public health can be part of the 
solution to this challenge. The evidence shows that prevention can be cost-effective, provide value for money and 
give returns on investment in both the short and longer terms. This public health summary outlines quick returns on 
investment for health and other sectors for interventions that promote physical activity and healthy employment; 
address housing and

summary.text: The report's abstract argues that, amid economic crisis and rising health costs, prevention can be cost-effective and give short- and long-term returns on investment. It highlights quick returns from interventions on physical activity, healthy employment, housing, mental health, road traffic injuries and violence, and notes population-level approaches cost much less than individual ones.

Key messages state that current costs of ill health are unsustainable and that many kinds of prevention are cost-effective in the short and longer term.

summary.text: Makes the economic case for prevention, arguing that health promotion and disease prevention offer value for money and can produce returns on investment and wider social benefits. It explains primary, secondary and tertiary prevention and argues that upstream population approaches reduce inequalities more effectively. It presents projections of rising public health care spending and estimates of the deaths, illness and costs caused by health inequalities in 25 European countries. The section introduces evidence tables on the cost of inaction and the cost-effectiveness of interventions across health areas.

summary.text: Presents a hierarchy of prevention from business as usual to cost-saving and return-on-investment interventions and a diagram of the report's summary tables. It reproduces WHO "best buy" tables by risk factor and by health outcome, with disease burden, cost-effectiveness, implementation cost and feasibility. Further tables summarise cost-effective interventions for resilience, social and environmental determinants, and vaccination and screening. It ends by stressing investment in modern health protection services, including communicable disease control, environmental health and emergency preparedness.

summary.text: Concludes that interventions on social and environmental determinants, resilience, healthy behaviours, screening and vaccination can be cost-effective, some with returns within one or two years. It warns that cuts to public health services in the European Region risk higher future costs and discusses funding through taxes, insurance and protected budgets. It notes the low per-person cost of WHO's core noncommunicable disease interventions and the benefit of clustering approaches such as safe urban design. The block ends with references and the list of WHO European Region member states.
